analysis.one_liner: Requires warning labels on toys with small parts, stating the ages they are unsafe for.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Consumer Product Safety Commission to write a rule requiring that any toy containing a small part carry a prominent warning label on its packaging. The label would have to state which ages of children the toy is not intended for and describe the specific hazard — for example, a choking risk — in capital letters starting with 'WARNING.' The commission had to issue the rule by January 1, 1992, and could enforce it using its existing powers under the Federal Hazardous Substances Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and caregivers buying toys for young children. Small parts are a leading choking hazard for toddlers, and the bill would have required manufacturers and importers to say on the box which ages a toy is dangerous for, making it easier to keep hazardous toys away from children under three.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directed the Consumer Product Safety Commission to issue a regulation, by January 1, 1992, requiring cautionary labels on any toy containing a small part that is made, sold, distributed, or imported into the United States.
The label had to state the ages of children for which the toy is not intended and describe the dangerous property of the toy and the hazardous consequences it can cause, such as choking.
Labels had to be prominently and conspicuously displayed on the packaging and accompanying materials, visible and in English, and include the word 'WARNING' in capital letters.
The commission could enforce the labeling requirement using any remedy available to it under the Federal Hazardous Substances Act.

analysis.who_pays: Toy manufacturers and importers of toys with small parts, who would bear the cost of printing compliant warning labels on packaging and accompanying materials for toys manufactured after enactment.

drawbacks.text: The requirement applies only to labeling, not to the toys themselves: a toy that poses a choking danger to a toddler could still be manufactured and sold, as long as the package warns about it. A caregiver who does not read or cannot read the English-language label gets no protection.
Toy makers and importers would bear the cost of redesigning packaging and descriptive materials to carry the mandated warning, a compliance cost for products manufactured after enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to families is real but modest: clearer, standardized warnings about which young ages a small-parts toy is unsafe for, at a time when choking on small parts is a leading cause of toy-related deaths in toddlers. The cost to industry is limited to packaging changes and label printing, since the bill bans nothing and leaves the toys themselves on shelves. The main honest criticism is that a label is a weak protection — it shifts responsibility onto the caregiver reading the box rather than removing the hazard — and it would not help anyone who misses the fine print or reads no English.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its consumer protection subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sam Gejdenson introduced the Toy Safety and Child Protection Act in the House on April 11, 1991, with 52 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced.
On April 22, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness — the last action recorded before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a companion Senate action, and died when the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Toy manufacturers and importers of small-parts toys, who never had to print mandatory age-specific hazard warnings on their packaging, are better off because the bill died. Parents shopping for toddlers did not get the warnings.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Toy makers; parents got no labels

for.name: Rep. Sam Gejdenson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 52 original cosponsors, 30 of whom joined at introduction.

for.name: 52 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support but no committee action followed.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee / Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 11, 1991 and sent it to subcommittee on April 22; the bill sat there for the remaining twenty months of the Congress and was never marked up or voted on.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 47 of the 52 cosponsors were Democrats, with 5 Republicans joining — and no Republican chamber leader ever moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to print mandatory age-specific hazard warnings on the packaging of every small-parts toy made or imported after enactment, at their expense. Blocking it meant no such requirement existed, and their interest in avoiding the mandate ran against the safety information parents would have received.
Retailers would have sold the same toys but with labeled packaging, facing little direct compliance burden since labeling falls on manufacturers. Any effect on them was secondary and modest.
